list.listitem: To prevent injury, be aware of adverse weather, designate one team member to monitor other team members or use buddy system, dress and act appropriately in cold conditions. C
Classify frostbite based on superficial appearance and symptoms. Hemorrhagic blebs and lack of pain after thawing suggest deep tissue injury. C
Avoid freeze-refreeze cycles, and rapidly rewarm in a water bath. C
Medical therapy includes ibuprofen 6 mg/kg/dose twice daily, topical aloe vera gel on unroofed blebs, the prostacyclin iloprost, and antibiotics for infection. C
Selectively use thrombolytics, iloprost and surgical debridement or amputation for severe (3rd or 4th degree) frostbite injuries. B
Good health status of patient prior to injury improves prognosis (no malnutrition, vascular disease, neuropathy, dehydration, or other risk factors). C

background.definition: Frostbite involves tissue injury when ice crystallization of fluid occurs in the skin or subcutaneous or deeper tissue after exposure to subfreezing temperatures.

list.listitem: The annual incidence of frostbite in mountaineers was 366/1000/year in a 2005 survey of 637 mountaineers.
In 2004, the lifetime prevalence in Finnish men was reported as 44% to 48%, and the annual incidence as 2%; 12% had severe injury at some point in their lives.
In the U.S. Army, the incidence of hospitalization has decreased from 38/100,000 in 1985 to 0.2/100,000 in 1999; the crude overall incidence in 2019 was 36.5/100,000.
In a general full-time practice in a location predisposed to cold weather injuries there is approximately one case per year of frostbite.
In areas with cold recreational activities (sports, military training), several cases per year are common. Many patients do not seek medical attention.
Exposure to temperature less than or equal to −2°C (28°F).
Phase 1, cooling and freezing: tissue damage and cell death from frostbite due to crystallization of tissue fluids and extracellular ice crystal formation.
Phase 2, thawing and rewarming: later, vascular and inflammatory changes accompany rewarming.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Altered mental status (e.g., alcohol and substance abuse, head injury, dementia, psychiatric condition)
Lack of knowledge of dealing with the cold
Lack of appropriate clothing and equipment for the cold exposure
Decreased circulation or decreased sensation due to systemic diseases (e.g., arteriosclerotic vascular disease, diabetes, neuropathies)
Drugs or medication (e.g., nicotine, vasoconstrictive medicines)

list.listitem: Have knowledgeable personnel screen workers in a cold environment or create a "buddy system", and be aware of current and upcoming weather forecasts.C
Educate patients to avoid future insult, since tissue with prior cold damage is more prone to repeated and worse cold injury.C
Use appropriate clothing and equipment, which may be unique to one's risk for cold exposure especially of hands, feet, nose, and ears.C
Keep clothing dry and avoid over-heating, perspiring, and freezing.C
Frostbite is tissue damage due to freezing of tissue fluids causing a cold, numb, white, and waxy skin. Tissue with deep injury may demonstrate little subcutaneous tissue resilience. C
Thawing usually causes significant pain, gradual return of sensation, tissue edema, clear or hemorrhagic bullae, and superficial skin damage with possible deep tissue injury and gangrene. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Painful, pruritic, red-purplish papules, plaques, or nodules affecting fingers, toes, ears, and nose, appearing within 24 hours of cold exposure, resolving 1-2 weeks post-exposure, often with blistering, ulceration, or crusting in severe cases
Pain, pallor, and numbness of skin with cold exposure (similar to 1st degree frostbite), with full return of sensation and no tissue damage after warming

Differential.Differential_Name: Trench foot or immersion foot (nonfreezing cold injury)
Differential.Differential_Features: Early stage presents with cool, mottled, pale, numb feet; middle stage with petechiae and well-demarcated, painful, red-brown patches on the sole; late stage with edema, desquamation, ulceration, and gangrene
Transient, well-demarcated, pale or cyanotic cutaneous patches affecting the digits during cold exposure, which rapidly reverses upon warming

list.listitem:
The Wilderness Medical Society classifies frostbite according to 4 degrees:
1st degree: numbness and erythema, mild edema, no gross tissue infarction. 2nd degree: superficial skin vesiculation, with clear or milky fluid in the blisters, surrounded by erythema and edema. 3rd degree: deeper hemorrhagic blisters are present, indicating injury into the reticular dermis. 4th degree: injury extending through the dermis and to the level of bone.
1st and 2nd degree injuries are classified as "superficial," with no or minimal anticipated tissue loss.
3rd and 4th degree injuries are "deep," with likely tissue loss.

Patients present with a history of freezing temperatures and exposure, plus pain and especially numbness. A pale, waxy, cold, white body part supports the diagnosis, but not the amount of damage. Find out type of exposure, including the temperature, duration of exposure, and any history of previous injury or risk factors.
At first, patients will complain of numb, cold, waxy skin after exposure with subcutaneous tissue being soft and pliable to little or no resilience. There is usually pain with thawing.
Various levels of tissue destruction from superficial skin to deep tissues may be present simultaneously in one skin area.
Tissue destruction is characterized by edema, blister or vesicle formation, loss of epidermis to deep tissues with gangrene and permanent tissue loss.

Clear blebs or vesicle formation indicate less severe injury than bloody blebs or vesicle formation. Classification is generally not useful since all degrees of injury are initially treated the same until wound condition and tissue damage no longer deteriorates or improves.

Technitium scintigraphy, digital subtraction angiography, or magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) may help determine whether circulation is intact in the affected tissue and correlates with the likelihood of amputation.
Begin by getting history of exposure and symptoms, examine patient for other injuries or injury precipitants, and be aware that hypothermia often accompanies frostbite and localized cold injury.

Rewarm in 99°F to 102°F (37°C-39°C) bath for 20 to 45 minutes or until flushing occurs. 1st degree: minimal skin changes and erythema. Home care is generally adequate. 2nd degree: clear fluid-filled blebs, swelling, and pain. Home care is recommended for patients with sufficient home resources; hospitalization should be considered for those without. 3rd or 4th degree: deep tissue injury with proximal hemorrhagic blebs; no swelling, no pulses. Hospitalization is recommended.
Evidence-based guidelines are available online from the Wilderness Medical Society.
Laboratory tests and studies are usually not required.
Avoid freeze-refreeze cycles, and rapidly rewarm in a water bath. Do not rupture blebs.C
Medical therapy includes ibuprofen 6 mg/kg/dose twice daily, topical aloe vera gel on unroofed blebs, the prostacyclin iloprost, and antibiotics for infection.C
Selectively use thrombolytics, iloprosts and surgical debridement or amputation for severe (3rd or 4th degree) frostbite injuries.B

listitem.strong: Iloprost and thrombolysis for severe frostbite

list.listitem: A meta-analysis of 71 studies with 978 cases of frostbite concluded that iloprost given within 48 hours was effective for severe frostbite, and thrombolytics given within 24 hours were effective.

Thrombolytic therapy, using intraarterial or intravenous tissue plasminogen activator (tPA), is recommended for patients with 3rd or 4th degree frostbite within the first 24 hours after thawing when appropriate monitoring is available. A recent meta-analysis concluded that thrombolysis may reduce amputation after severe frostbite, but acknowledged that more rigorous trials with longer follow-up are needed.

A small historically controlled study compared iloprost alone given between 2000 and 2012 with iloprost + hyperbaric oxygen in the next 7 years. There were better outcomes with the combination therapy but this is very weak evidence.

A small open label RCT randomized 47 patients with severe (deep) frostbite into 3 groups: (1) aspirin + buflomedil, (2) aspirin + iloprost, and (3) aspirin, iloprost and fibrinolysis with recombinant tissue plasminogen activator. The rate of amputation was 60% in group 1, 0% in group 2, and 19% in group 3. The dose of iloprost was 0.5 to 2 ng/kg/min for 6 hours per day. A Cochrane review of interventions for frostbite injury found no additional randomized trials.

Some advocate prophylactic antibiotics for the first 48 to 72 hours, but this has not been shown to be superior to starting when signs of infection appear, there is an apparent source of infection, or if there has been major trauma.

Provide pain medication prior to and after rewarming and as indicated throughout treatment. Begin with NSAIDs like ibuprofen at a starting dose of 6 mg/kg/dose twice daily, with a maximum dose of 2400mg/day in 4 divided doses.

An early, small RCT suggested that nifedipine was more effective than placebo in decreasing the healing time of cutaneous lesions and reducing pain in patients with pernio. However, a more recent double-blind, crossover RCT of 32 patients with chronic perniosis found no difference in patient-reported pain or disability between nifedipine 30mg twice daily and placebo after 6 weeks of treatment. Ultraviolet therapy and vitamin D3 appear ineffective.

A recent randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind, crossover study of 34 patients with chronic chilblains did not find any benefit for topical betamethasone valerate 0.1% cream twice daily over placebo.

Oral pentoxyfylline for primary perniosis was studied in a double-blind, placebo-controlled, randomized trial enrolling 110 patients. Oral pentoxyfylline 400mg three times a day for 3 weeks showed faster resolution of skin lesions and pain compared to placebo at day 7, 14 and 21 (p = 0.015) with no side effects reported.
Observe and do not rupture blebs or blisters that appear.
Debride any spontaneously or accidentally ruptured vesicles under sterile conditions, using care to avoid damage to fragile tissues.

Delay amputation as long as possible. Serial examination, along with local wound care, is often sufficient to delineate viable from nonviable tissue, but MRI or technetium-99 bone scan may be considered if clinical uncertainty remains.
Patients in need of surgical interventions like debridement or amputation should be referred to hand surgery, plastic surgery, or podiatry.
Remove patient from continued exposure to prevent further freezing. Do not prematurely thaw if there is a possibility of refreezing. Thawing and refreezing increase damage over no thawing.

In the field, assess for hypothermia and other injury or illness. Remove any jewelry or clothing, and treat pain with ibuprofen or aspirin. Ibuprofen 6 mg/kg/dose twice daily may prevent tissue damage through its effect on the arachidonic acid pathway. Low molecular weight dextran can be given in the field to reduce blood viscosity, based on results of animal trials, but human trials are lacking. Do not apply dressings and avoid ambulation unless it is unavoidable at which point immobilization and padding are recommended.

Rapidly rewarm the affected body part or the entire patient for 20 to 45 minutes in water bath of 99°F to 102°F (37°C-39°C) until sensation reappears. Do not add an antiseptic to the water. Pain after rewarming generally means that the tissue is viable. After rewarming, allow the area to dry to the exposed air; do not towel or rub dry. Rewarming can be done in the field if more than 2 hours from medical facilities, and refreezing can be confidently avoided.

The 2024 American Heart Association and American Red Cross Guidelines for First Aid recommend that if immersion is unavailable, spontaneous rewarming via room air or skin-to-skin contact is the preferred secondary method.

Following thawing, patient should be hospitalized and affected parts treated under sterile conditions, kept open, and patient placed under isolation. Allow to dry in open air, do not towel or rub dry. The appearance of blebs or blisters suggests deep superficial injury; hemorrhagic blebs indicate deep injury.
Elevate the affected extremity if possible to avoid edema, and give oxygen to maintain O2 saturation >90%.

Local daily or twice daily gentle, non-abrasive cleaning (preferrably with whirlpool type of water bath), air draping status post, protection of injury tissue from local or topical damage with gauze or cotton balls between injured digits.

The affected part should have active exercises of both large and small muscle groups and intermittent relaxation of the affected part when edema has decreased. Patients with frostbitten feet should remain non-ambulatory during recovery.
Observe all blebs (clear or bloody) and debride only if they rupture; avoid secondary infections with meticulous care.
Use a bulky, dry gauze dressing. Apply topical aloe vera gel to unroofed blebs with dressing changes, every 6 hours. Do not use wet dressings, occlusive dressings, or ointments.
Smoking cessation is recommended for patients who smoke. Tetanus prophylaxis needs to be administered, if indicated.
Hospitalize all patients with severe frostbite, consult a surgeon, and consult someone with experience in frostbite care if available.
Establish a system to rapidly evacuate patients with severe frostbite injuries to a treatment center.
Have the medical system establish protocols in the emergency department to limit tissue injury.

Watch for frostbite sequelae: cold sensitivity, hyperhidrosis, intrinsic muscle atrophy, skin color changes, arthritis, hyperesthesia, vasospastic attacks, growth retardation if growth plate abnormalities (in children), tissue loss, chronic pain, and others. C
Good health status of patient prior to injury appears to improve prognosis (no malnutrition, vascular disease, neuropathy, dehydration, or other risk factors). C
Prompt care by knowledgeable medical personnel likely improves outcome, whereas delayed care likely increases the risk of infection and tissue damage. C
Prognosis depends on the degree of cold injury and the promptness of treatment. C
